samples.text:
The bar chart compare how many litres of water one person use every day for six activities at home in Country A and Country B.

In Country A, shower and bath use the most water with 68 litres. Toilet is second with 45 litres, and garden is 40 litres. Laundry uses 32 litres, kitchen and drinking 18 litres and other activities 12 litres.

In Country B, people use much less water for all the activities. Shower and bath is also the highest, but it is only 30 litres, which is less than half of Country A. Toilet is 22 litres and laundry is 15 litres. Kitchen and drinking is 14 litres, and this is quite similar to Country A. The biggest difference is garden, because people in Country B only use 3 litres for it, but in Country A it is 40 litres.

Overall, Country A uses more water than Country B for every activity, and shower or bath is the activity which uses the most water in both countries.
samples.why: Figures accurate and key differences identified · overview basic and placed last · country-by-country listing with simple linking · repetitive vocabulary · several agreement and word-choice errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The chart compares the average amount of water used per person each day for six household activities in two countries, A and B.

Overall, people in Country A consumed considerably more water than those in Country B for every activity. In both countries, showering and bathing accounted for the largest amount, while the greatest difference between the two was in garden use.

In Country A, an average of 68 litres per person was used for showers and baths every day, more than twice the figure for Country B (30 litres). Similarly, toilet use and laundry in Country A required 45 and 32 litres respectively, roughly double the corresponding amounts in Country B, at 22 and 15 litres.

The contrast was most striking for gardens. Residents of Country A used 40 litres daily on their gardens, making it the third-largest category there, whereas in Country B the figure was just 3 litres, the lowest of any activity. By comparison, water used for the kitchen and drinking was fairly similar in two countries, at 18 litres and 14 litres, and other uses accounted for 12 litres in A and 6 in B.
samples.why: Clear overview of main differences · key features presented with accurate comparisons · logical paragraphing and a range of linkers · some less common collocations · mostly error-free with one article slip.

samples.text:
The bar chart compares daily domestic water consumption per person in two countries, broken down into six categories of use.

Residents of Country A used more water than those of Country B in every category, and in most cases around twice as much. Showers and baths were the largest single use in both countries, but the most dramatic disparity concerned gardening, which was a major use of water in Country A yet almost negligible in Country B.

Showering and bathing accounted for 68 litres per person per day in Country A, compared with 30 litres in Country B. A similar ratio applied to toilet use (45 and 22 litres), laundry (32 and 15 litres) and other purposes (12 and 6 litres), all of which were roughly twice as high in Country A.

Garden watering was the notable exception to this pattern. In Country A, it consumed 40 litres per person each day, placing it third among the six activities, whereas the equivalent figure in Country B was a mere 3 litres, the smallest amount on the chart. At the other end of the spectrum, kitchen use and drinking showed the least variation, at 18 litres in Country A and 14 litres in Country B.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected using ratios · clear overview · figures grouped efficiently for comparison · cohesion managed well · wide, precise vocabulary · complex sentences handled accurately.
